item.title: ‘A Dying Community’: An Energy Crisis Worsened by the War Strains Alaska
item.description:
One hundred miles south of the Arctic Circle, at the end of the Elliott Highway in the center of Alaska, Sabie Jervsjo has done everything she can to lower her energy bills.

She replaced the incandescent lightbulbs in her Manley Hot Springs home with LEDs, installed motion sensors and switched appliances from electricity to propane. She’s teaching her grandchildren to turn off the lights and decide what they want before opening the refrigerator.

But no amount of conservation can solve the problem that Ms. Jervsjo and tens of thousands of other Alaskans are facing. A state rich in oil is in the middle of an energy crisis worsened by a war on the other side of the planet.

More than 190 rural communities in Alaska depend on diesel for electricity and heat. Alaska pumps more than 400,000 barrels of crude oil a day, but much of the diesel burned in remote villages comes from crude drilled and refined in other parts of the world. Higher global oil prices boost state revenue, but they also drive up energy, heating and transportation costs in places that can least afford them.

Rural Alaskans are “having to choose between feeding their families and having a warm home,” said Dominique Pride, a deputy director for research at the Alaska Center for Energy and Power in Fairbanks. “We wouldn’t accept that in New York or Miami,” she added. “Why is it OK up here?”

The strain is coming in a heated political moment: One of the state’s senators, Dan Sullivan, a Republican, is locked in a tight race with a former Democratic representative, Mary Peltola, that could determine control of the Senate next year. Alaska’s lone House seat is competitive, and 17 people are running to be Alaska’s next governor. The high cost of living in rural Alaska is an issue in every race.

State lawmakers in Juneau, about 885 miles south of Ms. Jervsjo’s home, have spent months fighting over a proposed 800-mile natural gas pipeline from the North Slope to the “Railbelt” around Anchorage, where most Alaskans live. But that project would do nothing for farther-flung communities like Manley Hot Springs, which sits 155 miles west of Fairbanks at the edge of Alaska’s remote, rural interior.

The road to Manley is called a highway, but the pavement gives way to gravel and dirt about 80 miles before it ends at the Tanana River. Gold miners came first. Wealthy tourists followed for the hot springs. At its peak, around 5,000 people lived in the area. Now, about 75 year-round residents remain.

“It’s not a place you stumble across,” said Pam Redington, whose father-in-law helped found the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race. She arrived in 1977 with two children and 57 sled dogs.

People in Manley hold three or four jobs, and during the long winters, they gather for craft nights and dances at the tribal hall. Many still haul water from the community well and shower and do laundry at the town “washeteria.”

A local pilot first generated electricity with a diesel generator for his home and hangar in the late 1970s before gradually extending power lines through town. In 1981, when Ms. Redington wanted lights at her house a mile from the center of town, she had to buy the poles and dig the holes herself.

Like most rural Alaska communities, Manley is powered by a microgrid, with two diesel generators maintained by a staff of two, who also answer late-night outage calls and clear fallen trees after storms. Only one works full time.

Even with a state subsidy, electricity in Manley is among the most expensive in the country.

“You’re always thinking ahead: If I do this, it will cost me this. If I do this other thing, it will cost less,” said Heather Redington, Pam Redington’s daughter. “Every choice matters.”

A few years ago, Ms. Jervsjo’s household used around 700 kilowatt-hours of electricity a month, shy of the national average. That cost her between $500 and $600 each bill. Now, she tries to stay below 300 kilowatt-hours a month, enough to bring her bill down to $300 or even $250. In the winter, Ms. Jervsjo cooks on a wood stove.

“It’s everything I do, everywhere I go,” she said of her extreme conservation. “It’s the only way to afford to live.”

That requires real sacrifice in a place that sees only a few hours of twilight in winter and where wolves recently carried off a family dog.

Business owners, who aren’t covered by the state’s residential subsidies, have it even worse. John Dart farmed in Manley for 18 years but was paying more than $1 per kilowatt-hour — the average U.S. business pays 13 cents, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, and the average commercial rate in Alaska is about 26 cents.

Mr. Dart’s monthly electric bill exceeded $1,000. Combined with $7-a-gallon diesel for his delivery truck, even his experiments in geothermal heating wasn’t helpful enough. He and his wife let their farm go fallow this summer.

“I can’t lose tens and tens and tens of thousands of dollars,” he said.

Electricity is only half the equation. Heating is largely unsubsidized in rural Alaska, and Manley homeowners typically burn hundreds, sometimes thousands, of gallons of diesel each winter. That’s where the wars in Iran and Ukraine have brought the biggest pain. Every family must truck in its own fuel before the cold arrives.

The Elliott Highway winds over mountains and through forests and can turn into a mud track in the summer and an ice sheet in the winter. Many residents make the four-hour drive to Fairbanks several times each summer to stock up, and most try to return the same day to avoid hotel prices.

How much to buy is a guessing game. Last winter, after three weeks when temperatures never rose above 50, Ms. Redington ran out of heating oil and had to buy more in Manley, where fuel costs 23 percent more. A few hundred dollars can be life-altering in Manley, where the median age is 75 and most live on fixed incomes.

When much of rural Alaska was electrified in the second half of the 20th century, building on military power grids from World War II, diesel generators were the obvious choice as they were inexpensive, reliable and easy to maintain. Few questioned whether villages scattered across Alaska should depend almost entirely on a product that had to be imported and, in many cases, delivered by seasonal barge or airplane.

Now some reminisce about the days before electricity.

“We got along without it,” Ms. Jervsjo said. “We could do it again if we had to.”

State agencies, utilities and nonprofits are experimenting with solar, wind and hydroelectric projects and battery storage to reduce diesel use and extend generator life. In late 2023, TDX Power installed a solar array with battery storage in Manley. In the sun-filled summer, the system can power the village for more than half a day while the diesel generators sit idle.

But residents mostly notice what hasn’t changed: high power bills and frequent outages.

“There is no silver bullet,” said Curtis Thayer, executive director of the Alaska Energy Authority.

Rural Alaska is important, even if “you get the sense some people wouldn’t care if places like this disappeared,” Ms. Jervsjo said.

The vast hinterlands hold the nation’s most promising sources of fossil fuel and rare earth minerals, vital to high-tech, military contractors and even the auto industry. Miners, drillers and the military will need villages in hard-to-reach places as base camps, just like the miners who first settled in Manley.

“This is not just about doing the right thing,” said Ben Mallott, president of the Alaska Federation of Natives, which serves 192 federally recognized tribes and 152 village corporations. “Having those communities in there, it’s a national security matter.”

Their continued existence isn’t guaranteed. Built in 1903, the Manley Roadhouse is still the social hub of Manley Hot Springs, cluttered with photos of old sled dog races and taxidermied animals.

A mining crew surveying soil for future projects around Manley has made the roadhouse its home for much of this summer. Still, Pam Redington, now 80, worries about the town’s future. Most residents are older, there are few full-time jobs, and the local school closed in 2019 because Manley didn’t have the 10 children needed to meet the state minimum. High energy prices, with no relief in sight, are one more reason to leave.

“In a way, it’s a dying community,” Ms. Redington said. “I’m worried we’re going to have to put up a sign that says, ‘Last person out, shut off the light.’”

item.title: Is Activism Hurting Sociology? Sociologists Are Torn.
item.description:
The president of the major sociology association, Shelley Correll, had just taken the stage at the discipline’s big annual conference in New York City on Sunday when a few dozen sociologists began chanting “Free Palestine” and unfurled a banner.

The short disruption was partly drowned out by turning up Dr. Correll’s entrance music, Dolly Parton’s “Big Dreams and Faded Jeans.”

Tuning out the broader cacophony around sociology is not so easy, however.

Republicans in some states have singled out sociology as a poster child of everything that is wrong with academia, saying that it has become a hotbed of leftist activism. And rifts have formed within the discipline over whether to take political stances on issues like the war in Gaza.

At the same time, fewer students are signing up for sociology classes, making the debates feel all the more urgent.

Sociologists study human society and behavior. The field has long included a mix of science and activism. But sociology’s difficulties are driving arguments about whether the discipline should rein in its advocacy wing to gain public confidence, or stand its ground against outside attack.

“We lost something through this pursuit of partisanship,” said Fabio Rojas, a professor at Indiana University who writes about schisms in sociology, adding, “There are a lot of people who are just like, ‘I want to go to work and not hear about Palestine.’”

Sociology is sprawling. It includes ethnographers who conduct in-depth interviews, data-driven researchers and those who do both. Many sociologists study crime, demography, religion and other topics that do not generally irk conservatives. Sociology has also become a home for scholars who examine sexism, racism, policing, immigration and other politically charged topics.

The field emerged from the Enlightenment as a way to study human society and behavior amid rapid social change. Scrutinizing power was always a key part of the science, with early sociologists like W.E.B. Du Bois, Jane Addams and Harriet Martineau using scholarship to fight against racism, sexism and inequality.

Critics of the discipline say that it is now too hyper-focused on left-leaning concerns like inequality. That word appeared 186 times in the 165-page conference program.

Many sociologists argue that it’s impossible to study human society deeply without seeing inequality and discrimination. And those who support activism argue that it is not a big step to then use that knowledge to push for public policy changes.

The work of Anthony Abraham Jack, a Boston University sociologist, would be labeled activism by some. He wrote an impactful book called “The Privileged Poor,” about food insecurity among students at elite colleges. He then successfully pushed for schools to change their dining-hall policies.

Dr. Jack prefers the term “public scholarship.” He says that his work “is expanding the definition of what scholarship is, to not just publish articles and write books but also to be part of the dissemination of information.” He and other sociologists argue that economists, for instance, might advocate their preferred policy positions but aren’t thought of as “activists.”

But critics of the state of the discipline say sociologists who aim to change the conditions they study can no longer claim to be rigorous scientists. A report released over the weekend about the state of scholarly standards in the field said it had been compromised by politics that influenced the discipline’s values and priorities.

The report was produced by a commission led by Vanderbilt University and Washington University in St. Louis, where leaders have argued that higher education is in need of reforms. The commission found that scholarship in the humanities and social sciences was sometimes in the service of political goals.

“Some topics cannot be studied or cannot be studied in an honest way,” said Jukka Savolainen, a Wayne State University criminologist and sociologist who is not part of the commission.

For scholars studying incarceration, he said, “the only research that’s rewarded and allowed and encouraged is to find the umpteenth way in which incarceration is harmful.”

Other academic disciplines like history and anthropology face many of the same accusations of a left-wing bias. But conservatives in Florida singled out sociology in their push to excise what they said were left-leaning topics from the college curriculum.

Sociology courses are no longer allowed in the required general-education curriculum, a move that has sociology professors fearful that enrollments could plummet in the fall.

Ray Rodrigues, the head of the State University System of Florida, has said that the discipline is “now social and political advocacy dressed in the regalia of the academy.”

Scott Yenor, a conservative activist who briefly served on the board of the University of West Florida, said sociology had acquired a reputation as being left-wing for decades but that there were also strategic reasons it had been singled out by conservatives.

“History can be as bad,” said Dr. Yenor, a Boise State University political scientist, “but going after history makes you seem like you’re anti-intellectual. Conservatives like history.”

The sociology conference’s theme this year played to the scholar-activism wing: “Disrupting the Status Quo: Putting Sociology to Work for a More Equitable Society.” Republicans cited it as further evidence that the discipline was overrun with activism.

Dr. Correll, a Stanford sociologist, picked the theme and defended the scholar-activist model.

In an interview, Dr. Correll, who studies gender inequality in the workplace, said that many people became sociologists “to help make the world a better place.” She added that she had chosen the Dolly Parton song because it “offers a hopeful and compelling blueprint for social change.”

Student interest in sociology has dramatically dropped in recent decades. One analysis found that since 2013, completions of undergraduate sociology degrees fell by 25 percent.

Sociologists cite factors like a broader societal shift toward degrees that are perceived as prioritizing trade skills. The political attacks do not help.

While concerned sociologists worry that embracing activism could drive away new recruits to the discipline, some say that staying true to the discipline’s social justice roots will be what saves it.

The overall numbers mask that sociology is thriving in some liberal places, especially California. An analysis by Michel Estefan, a sociologist at the University of California, San Diego, found that two out of every five sociology bachelor’s degrees were earned in California.

The majority of them are students of color. Scholars like Dr. Estefan see a racial component in how quickly researchers are described and dismissed as “activists.” One person’s “activism” is another’s “policy recommendation,” he said.

At the New York conference, fissures over Gaza were the main point of division, not whether sociologists should dial down their activism more broadly.

Close to a thousand sociologists boycotted this year’s event because the group’s leadership did not allow a membership vote on whether to admonish and boycott Israel, according to the boycott’s organizers. More than 4,500 sociologists attended the main conference, officials said. Some attended a shadow conference down the street titled, “Resisting Authoritarianism: Global Solidarity and Democratic Futures.”

Dr. Correll said she did not see how boycotting Israel would make a difference in Gaza.

But Zachary Levenson, a sociologist at Florida International University who is a member of Sociologists for Palestine, said the scholars’ activism was part of a broader movement started by student protesters that had made a difference. It caused “a sea change in public opinion” against Israel that Dr. Levenson said he had never seen before.

Dr. Levenson rejected the notion that the Gaza activism was hurting the discipline’s public perception. It was Dr. Correll, he said, who had embraced “quite literally the politicization of the field” by embracing scholarly advocacy — except on the Gaza issue.

Dr. Correll said she wasn’t worried. She said the disagreement was a sign of pluralism, and that the discipline had overcome major challenges before.

“It’s really healthy for an academic discipline to not be grounded into just one way of being,” she said.

item.title: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Greenlight White House Ballroom
item.description:
The Trump administration on Friday asked the Supreme Court to bless the construction of President Trump’s White House ballroom to replace the demolished East Wing.

The planned 90,000-square-foot ballroom has been mired in litigation ever since the president tore down the East Wing in October as part of his plan to dramatically remake the White House campus. But the courts have let Mr. Trump build even while questioning the project’s legality, allowing the ballroom to steadily rise in recent months.

The administration’s request for intervention from the nation’s highest court comes after an appeals court said on Aug. 7 that the president had most likely exceeded his authority by moving ahead with the privately financed project without approval from Congress. The case poses a test of the limits of executive authority for a Supreme Court that has embraced some, but not all, of the president’s agenda. It also presents the justices with yet another challenge to one of Mr. Trump’s signature initiatives.

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, told the justices on Friday that the project was already 65 percent complete and suggested it was too late to stop construction. A 250-person crew has been working 20 hours a day, seven days a week to build a concrete-and-steel superstructure that now stretches five stories deep and 70 feet high, he said.

“Halting the project will stall this vital construction, making this president — the subject of recurrent assassination attempts — much less safe, and risking future presidents’ safety,” he wrote in the Friday filing.

In its 2-to-1 ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit said the Constitution gives Congress — not the president — the responsibility to decide when proposed changes to the White House may move ahead.

“Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the executive branch to dramatically redesign, reshape and reconstruct the White House — the People’s House — to fit a particular president’s desires,” the appeals court ruled.

The appeals court had paused its ruling for two weeks to give Mr. Trump time to appeal to the Supreme Court. His petition landed a week later. In the interim, work on the project continued.

Mr. Sauer asked the justices to immediately pause the appeals court ruling, which would halt construction as of Aug. 21. He said the secure ballroom space and an underground military complex were “vitally required for national security.”

Construction of the ballroom, estimated to cost $400 million, is part of Mr. Trump’s second-term effort to reshape Washington in his style. Stopping the project now, Mr. Sauer said Friday, would leave an incomplete structure in place that would be susceptible to “strong winds during extreme weather, and vulnerable to erosion, water, foundation damage” and other setbacks.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation, a nonprofit chartered by Congress to guard America’s historic buildings, sued to try to stop the ballroom’s construction, asserting that the president had resisted oversight in violation of federal law.

Mr. Trump has defended the project, insisting that congressional approval is not necessary and that his plans are no different than previous, more modest renovation projects completed at the White House without consultation with lawmakers. He has said the White House is in need of a large event facility; state dinners and other big events have long been held in tents outdoors because of the lack of such a space.

The president’s legal team has shifted its claims about the project since the litigation began, asserting in recent months that its primary purpose is to add a sprawling underground military complex to improve White House security.

In its filing on Friday, the administration’s lawyers said the trust lacks legal grounds or standing to bring the lawsuit because it does not have a “personal or financial stake” in the outcome.

After the appeals court ruling, Mr. Trump said on social media that “this unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety.” He emphasized that the project was vital for national security and military operations.

In April, Judge Richard J. Leon of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ruled that the project exceeded the scale of the kind of minor changes presidents have traditionally made to the White House grounds and required approval from Congress. The judge, however, deferred to the president’s claims about the critical need for an upgrade of the military bunker below the White House. His ruling, upheld by the appeals court, would halt construction of the ballroom but allow renovations below ground to continue, including construction of bunkers, bomb shelters, and military and medical infrastructure.

Despite that ruling, Judge Leon permitted construction to continue temporarily both above and below ground while the litigation played out.

The National Capital Planning Commission, which reviews plans for major projects and renovations, voted to approve the project in April. The president had installed allies on the commission before announcing a design for the ballroom.

The project is being funded by private donations. Democrats and public interest groups have raised conflict-of-interest concerns about the financing because many corporate donors engage in business with the federal government.

Mr. Trump has said that the private funds give him the flexibility to pursue the project at no expense to taxpayers, and that he does not need congressional approval for the overhaul of the White House when taxpayer money is not involved.

But in June, the administration transferred roughly $350 million from the Secret Service to cover security upgrades at the White House, which appeared to be destined for the combined East Wing project.

Seven Republican senators joined Democrats in June in voting to block the construction on the project until Congress had formally authorized it, but the measure failed to secure the 60 votes needed to pass.

item.title: Trump Pressured Russell Fry to Endorse Darline Graham for Senate. So He Did.
item.description:
At the urging of President Trump, Representative Russell Fry of South Carolina has endorsed Senator Darline Graham after losing his bid in the special primary election on Tuesday to succeed her late brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, according to a person familiar with his thinking.

Mr. Fry announced the endorsement on Friday, throwing his weight behind Ms. Graham as she competes in a two-week runoff contest against Representative Ralph Norman, a longtime lawmaker and vice chairman of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus, in the solidly Republican state.

”President Trump needs fighters and allies in the Senate who will show up every day and get results,” Mr. Fry said in a statement. “I believe Darline Graham will be exactly that.”

Mr. Trump has been heavily involved in the race since Mr. Graham, his longtime ally, died unexpectedly in July. He endorsed Ms. Graham, a disability rights advocate who had never held political office, in the primary election after initially signaling he would support Mr. Fry. The runoff is scheduled for Aug. 25.

The president’s personal interest in the race reflects his close relationship with Mr. Graham and his focus on selecting a loyal ally to replace the late senator — especially in a year when Republicans are concerned about defending their majority in Congress. Although few see the seat at risk of flipping in the deeply red state, Mr. Trump has repeatedly dismissed the prospect of Mr. Norman, who endorsed Nikki Haley for president and is not seen as a reliable ally, filling the seat.

Since polls closed in the primary election on Tuesday, Mr. Trump has been working the phones to drum up support for Ms. Graham, according to three people familiar with the calls who were granted anonymity to discuss private conversations.

That night, Mr. Trump called Mr. Fry to encourage him to endorse Ms. Graham, one of the people said.

Mr. Trump lavished the congressman with praise and stressed that he saw a bright future for him, one of the people said.

Mr. Fry had been torn about whether to endorse Ms. Graham, in part because the bitterly fought primary left a bad taste between the two candidates and their political teams, as both sides sought to sell their alignment with the president, one of the people said.

During the primary campaign, Mr. Fry’s team cast Ms. Graham as supportive of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and sharply criticized her encouragement of building data centers in the state.

Mr. Fry ultimately decided to prioritize loyalty to the president, the person said.

Mr. Fry called Mr. Trump on Thursday night to discuss the endorsement again. On that call, the person said, Mr. Fry encouraged Mr. Trump to visit the Myrtle Beach area, his hometown, and rally in support of Ms. Graham.

item.title: She Sewed the Blue Angels’ Suits for 40 Years. Then a Big Company Got the Job.
item.description:
For nearly 40 years, the Blue Angels, the Navy pilots renowned for performing acrobatic moves at air shows and other events across the country, have turned to Jellie Whitehurst, who is known as Candy, to make their blue-and-yellow flight suits.

But last month, Ms. Whitehurst said, she was blindsided. She reached out to an officer from the flying team about paying a visit to take measurements for new suits. It was only then, she said, that the officer told her she would not be making them anymore.

The Navy, she learned, had awarded the contract to a much larger company, a defense contractor in Virginia, far from the Blue Angels’ base in Pensacola, Fla., and her nearby tailoring shop, The Sewing Box, on North Navy Boulevard.

“It was devastating to lose it. Period,” she said. “But it was even more devastating to lose it like this. I would have never thought my Blues would do me like this — that they would treat me like this when we had a good relationship.”

She said that the Blue Angels had always come directly to her to submit a bid as the sole supplier of the suits, and that the officers there never told her they were soliciting other bids to make the suits.

Cmdr. Amber Lewis, a spokeswoman for Navy Supply Systems Command, said in a statement that Ms. Whitehurst had informed the Blue Angels in January “that it was her intention to retire.”

“The following month, the formal, open process of posting, bidding and awarding the contract for the next supplier of Blue Angels uniforms was started and completed several months later in accordance with federal law,” she said.

Ms. Whitehurst, who declined to give her age, contests that claim. She said she never told the Blue Angels — or anyone else — that she was retiring.

“I am not planning to retire,” she said.

The change in contractors was reported earlier by a Pensacola news station, WEAR-TV, and by Stars and Stripes.

After Ms. Whitehurst broke down in tears as she discussed the issue on CNN this week, some social media users speculated that race might have been a factor.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has taken steps to eliminate diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts, including programs intended to assist small businesses owned by minorities.

Ms. Whitehurst’s past contract documents for the Blue Angels’ suits noted that The Sewing Box is a small, woman- and minority-owned business.

She said she believed the woman- and minority-owned designations were not factors in her having won contracts to make the suits, and she was not sure why the Navy had chosen another vendor.

“They wanted me, and they knew I could do it,” she said in an interview. “My quality was the factor.”

Making flight suits for the Blue Angels has long been a handmade, bespoke process.

After measuring each member of the team, Ms. Whitehurst said, she draws the patterns for their suits on craft paper and cuts out the pieces from a 100-yard roll of flame-resistant Nomex fabric.

Using Nomex thread, she stitches them together with a belt, pockets and zippers, adds the Blue Angels insignia and embroiders the name and rank of each member in yellow. Each custom-fitted suit takes about five and a half hours to make, and she estimated the cost at $850 per suit. She said she makes 85 to 100 suits each year.

“It’s a lot of joy and pride that I feel that the world sees something I made,” Ms. Whitehurst said.

Commander Lewis said a notice seeking potential vendors was posted on Jan. 29 on sam.gov, a government contracting website, and remained open until Feb. 18, allowing vendors to submit information about their capabilities and experience. Aquila International, a government contractor in Dulles, Va., was awarded the contract on May 14.

“Sewing Box was not among those who submitted bids on the open and transparent process,” Commander Lewis said. “The contract was awarded to best value to the government. The cost per uniform is less than the previous contract.”

Ms. Whitehurst started working at The Sewing Box in 1989. She learned the craft of making the Blue Angels’ tightfitting suits with Samuel Miller, a former Navy officer who opened the shop in about 1978.

He had initially called it Feminine Flair and had planned to make women’s dresses.

“That was kind of the wrong name to pick,” Mr. Miller, who died in 2022, told The Pensacola News Journal in 2019. “Pensacola is not a trendsetting city, as you might know, so that did not work out. I had to very quickly mutate and went into alterations and uniforms.”

Since 2014, the Sewing Box has earned $684,000 from the Navy to make the suits, according to usaspending.gov, a government website that tracks federal spending. The Navy’s new five-year contract with Aquila International is worth $1.69 million.

Commander Lewis did not explain the cost difference, but her statement said: “For all bids, technical factors were considered as well as cost in the evaluation process.”

Todd Kelsey, a founder of Aquila International, told WEAR that he was proud his company had won the bid. He noted that the company had been making other items for the Blue Angels since 2024, including flight gloves and compression garments.

Aquila International said it has other federal contracts, such as supplying tactical gear and first-aid kits for the State Department. In a statement, it said that its “focus now is ensuring a seamless transition and delivering exceptional uniforms and equipment for the Blue Angels.”

Ms. Whitehurst said she still hoped to win back the contract. She has been consulting with a lawyer, but said she was not sure if she would take legal action.

“It would mean a lot to me if I could get them back,” she said. “And when I retire — when I decide to retire — I would like to retire as the maker of the flight suits.”

item.title: Mary Morello, Free Speech Activist Who Defended Explicit Lyrics, Dies at 102
item.description:
Mary Morello, a fiery anti-censorship activist — and the mother of the Rage Against the Machine guitarist Tom Morello — who rose to prominence in the 1980s as a leading opponent of Tipper Gore’s campaign against supposedly salacious artists like Prince and Madonna, died on July 12 at her home in Los Angeles. She was 102.

She died after multiple recent hospitalizations for pneumonia, Mr. Morello said.

A fierce champion for a long list of left-wing causes over the years, Ms. Morello was “the most radical member of the Morello family,” Mr. Morello said in an interview. That was no small feat given his reputation as an outspoken member of a band known for its power-chord polemics against racism, police brutality and corporate greed, including lyrics like “I warm my hands upon the flames of the flag.”

Ms. Morello was an Illinois schoolteacher in her mid-60s when, with a nudge from her son, she retired to found Parents for Rock and Rap in 1987.

Her chief target was the Parents Music Resource Center, or P.M.R.C, started two years earlier by Mrs. Gore, the wife of Senator Al Gore of Tennessee, along with other prominent Washington women, to keep music that had what the group deemed offensive lyrics out of the hands of children.

Mrs. Gore, who served as second lady after her husband became vice president in 1993, became a national lightning rod after a much-publicized Senate hearing in 1985. She and her associates squared off against Frank Zappa and other champions of the outré over what the P.M.R.C. labeled “porn rock.”

Exhibit A was a collection of songs the group labeled the Filthy Fifteen. They included Prince’s lubricious “Darling Nikki” and “Into the Coven” by the Danish heavy metal band Mercyful Fate as well as MTV-friendly (if steamy) tunes like Madonna’s “Dress You Up” and Cyndi Lauper’s “She Bop,” an ode to female masturbation.

The P.M.R.C. lobbied for parental guidance stickers for such material and for record stores to hide prurient albums out of view. It also suggested a Hollywood-style rating system: X for explicit sex; D/A for drug or alcohol references; V for violence; and O for occult- or satanic-themed songs.

Ms. Morello — described by the Chicago Tribune columnist Eric Zorn as a “sweet old lady living in a small white house on a shady suburban street,” never mind her soft spot for Ice-T and Led Zeppelin — was outraged.

“She just couldn’t believe it that there were these stuffy Washington wives who were denying artistic freedom to musicians,” Mr. Morello said. “When I was growing up, there was a lot of Kiss and Alice Cooper being played in the house, and she realized that it was not corrupting my soul.”

Armed with more passion than cash — she started her grass roots organization with $100 — Ms. Morello organized letter-writing campaigns from supporters around the country, and pleaded her First Amendment case on CNN, “The Oprah Winfrey Show” and any other news outlet that would have her.

Her list of the “enemies of freedom” included not just the P.M.R.C., but also allied groups, including the National PTA and the American Medical Association.

“When censorship starts in a democracy,” Ms. Morello wrote in a letter published in The Tribune in 1990, “where does it stop?”

The debate erupted once again in 1989 with the release of the aptly titled “As Nasty as They Wanna Be,” a sex-filled scorcher from the Miami rap group 2 Live Crew that became the first record in American history to be declared legally obscene by a federal court, although the ruling was reversed on appeal in 1992.

“Racial and sexual epithets,” Mrs. Gore wrote in a 1990 editorial in The Washington Post addressing the broader topic, “whether screamed across a street or camouflaged by the rhythms of a song, turn people into objects less than human — easier to degrade, easier to violate, easier to destroy.”

Ms. Morello mounted a full-throated defense of the album. “Nobody speaks that way around me,” she told USA Today in 1990, “but I think it’s a person’s prerogative to speak the way they want. There must be lots of comics in nightclubs who speak similarly and they don’t get harassed.”

Mary Rose Morello, the eldest of three children, was born on Oct. 1, 1923, in Marseilles, Ill., about 80 miles southwest of Chicago. Her father, John Morello, was a tavern owner and later a bank director. Her mother, Gladys (Fitzgerald) Morello, was a nurse.

Her social advocacy started early. “In the 1930s, she helped feed hobos during the Great Depression and supported the coal miners’ struggle to organize,” Tom Morello said in a eulogy at her funeral. “In the 1940s, she helped raise war bonds to defeat the fascists in World War II.”

She received a bachelor’s degree in social studies from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1945, followed by a master’s degree in history from Loyola University Chicago.

Ms. Morello worked as a teacher in Rock Island, Ill., as well as Japan, Spain and West Germany before going to Kenya in 1961 on a teaching program sponsored by Columbia University. At that point, Kenya was coming out of the Mau Mau rebellion, an often-brutal guerrilla offensive against British rule; the country gained formal independence in 1963.

Although the fighters were branded as terrorists in the Western news media, Ms. Morello was a staunch supporter. “They were revolutionaries, anti-colonialists,” she said in a 2000 interview with The Tribune. “So was George Washington. Would George Washington scare you?”

She eventually began a relationship with Ngethe Njoroge, who was allied with the cause and went on to become Kenya’s ambassador to Britain. The couple never married, Tom Morello said, but after she became pregnant with Tom, Ms. Morello returned to the United States, first moving to Harlem.

She and her son eventually settled in Libertyville, Ill., about 40 miles north of Chicago, where she began teaching history and African studies at Libertyville High School.

In a small, conservative town, she and her biracial son faced discrimination. “Someone put a noose and Klan literature on my bulletin board at school,” she recalled in a 2020 interview with the site Elaine Sir.

During the 1980s, Mr. Morello graduated from Harvard and moved to Los Angeles, playing in the band Lock Up. From his position on rock’s front lines, he helped stoke his mother’s interest in the brewing censorship battle.

She ran Parents for Rock and Rap into the late 1990s, picking up friends like Bono, Joan Baez, Bruce Springsteen and Chuck D from the rap group Public Enemy.

In the end, her fight with Mrs. Gore and the others was something of a draw. The P.M.R.C. failed to institute a rating system, although black-and-white parental advisory stickers warning of explicit content became commonplace.

They also became an inadvertent marketing tool, according to many artists and label executives — a badge of authenticity that also turbocharged sales with the promise of forbidden fruit.

In 1996, Ms. Morello was awarded a Hugh M. Hefner First Amendment Award.

In addition to her son, she is survived by five grandchildren.

To celebrate her 100th birthday in 2023, Ms. Morello passed out food at the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles and showed up in a wheelchair to support striking hotel workers.

At his mother’s funeral, Mr. Morello related a story from his childhood, when his mother insisted they join a boycott of grapes led by the United Farm Workers and Cesar Chavez.

For her son, it was epiphany. “There was a new North Star, guiding my thought and action,” he said, “and it was the same one that guided my mom: We have to help those people because we can.”

item.title: Woman Charged With Vandalizing World War II Memorial
item.description:
The Justice Department charged a Kentucky woman with two federal felonies on Friday after U.S. Park Police officers said they observed her spray painting the World War II Memorial in Washington.

Melissa L. Farris, 41, of Elizabethtown, Ky., was charged with defacing federal property and destruction of a veterans’ memorial, according to a complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. In a social media post, Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, said Ms. Farris was facing jail time of up 10 years.

According to the criminal complaint, on Thursday afternoon, Ms. Farris used orange spray paint to write “Clean Hands Dirty $” on a section of the wall on the Atlantic pavilion of the memorial, where she also sprayed green and yellow paint and splattered pink paint on adjacent stones. A U.S. Park ranger who responded to the scene also noticed foam in the fountain nearby.

Ms. Farris fled the scene, according to the complaint. But a couple of hours later, the complaint said, she posted a video of herself to a Facebook account under the name Melissa Lovewell, saying, “I was just allowed to deface Federal [expletive] property, and nobody batted an eye.” In the video, she also guessed that police would be pursuing her.

In videos posted to the same account on Friday morning, a tearful woman who appears to be Ms. Farris said she intended to turn herself in to the authorities. Ms. Pirro announced on Friday morning that Ms. Farris was in custody.

The complaint notes that just before defacing the memorial, Ms. Farris posted another video to her Facebook account saying she was “cognitively aware” of her actions and was “doing so to push my whistle-blower case into the courtroom.” It was not immediately clear what that case may involve.

It was the second time that Ms. Farris had been arrested this week, according to the complaint, which noted that she was arrested on Monday just a few blocks north of the World War II Memorial for “unlawfully camping on federal property.” The complaint noted that she was livestreaming throughout that arrest on the same Facebook account.

item.title: Lawsuit Accuses Selena Gomez of Defrauding Investors in Mental Health Site
item.description:
Selena Gomez, the actress, singer and beauty mogul, has been accused of defrauding investors in her mental health start-up, according to a federal lawsuit filed on Thursday.

Ms. Gomez co-founded Wondermind, a mental health and wellness platform, with her mother, Mandy Teefey, who is also a defendant in the lawsuit, in 2021, to make mental health content more accessible. But investors say the founders “falsely represented” the infrastructure, leadership and resources of the start-up, according to the lawsuit filed in Delaware.

Investors, represented by two separate limited liability companies, said Ms. Gomez and her mother had directly solicited nearly $1.2 million from them. They purchased $425,000 of preferred stock in May 2022 and $750,000 in June 2022.

The plaintiffs said they had been told that Ms. Gomez would be “actively building the company as its head of marketing,” that she signed a contract “obligating her to perform and then ignored it.” Promised partnerships with J.P. Morgan and Fidelity, in which Wondermind would provide mental health and wellness services to their employees, “did not exist”; advertising deals, celebrity cover stories and a “groundbreaking app” never materialized, the lawsuit says.

While Wondermind “quietly collapsed around them, not one of its founders, officers, or directors said a word to the investors,” the lawsuit says.

The investors said they instead learned about the “utter financial and operational disarray at Wondermind” from a story in The Cut published in September 2025. The story included allegations of substance abuse among leadership; Ms. Gomez’s efforts to distance herself from the company; the ouster of its chief executive, Daniella Pierson; and failure to pay its employees or vendors. Ms. Gomez has long been open about her mental health struggles.

Wondermind began as a website, with plans to create a “mental fitness ecosystem,” including an editorial publication, a mobile app and a podcast, with Ms. Gomez to “remain intimately involved,” the lawsuit said.

But Ms. Gomez, Ms. Teefey and Ms. Pierson, who is also named in the lawsuit, concealed issues and defrauded the investors by claiming that Wondermind “was performing well and poised for success,” the lawsuit said.

Ms. Pierson said in a statement that she “categorically denies the allegations against her and welcomes the opportunity to present concrete documentation and financial records that establish the facts.” She denied using investor funds for personal expenses.

Representatives for Ms. Gomez and Ms. Teefey did not return a request for comment.

During its first round of funding, Wondermind’s leaders told potential investors that it had an initial valuation of $95 million, and was seeking a $5 million investment. Ms. Gomez, Ms. Teefey and Ms. Pierson collectively controlled about 90 percent of Wondermind’s shares, the lawsuit said. Ms. Pierson told investors that Wondermind could have a potential value of over $4 billion, in large part because of Ms. Gomez’s involvement and celebrity.

Wondermind marketed Ms. Pierson, the founder of The Newsette, an online media company, as “a rising star,” according to the lawsuit. Ms. Pierson left Wondermind in 2023, which the plaintiffs believed at the time was “a voluntary departure,” according to the lawsuit.

But last August, Forbes published a story that included claims about Ms. Pierson exaggerating her experience and success with The Newsette. When the plaintiffs contacted Ms. Teefey for an explanation, she told them that Ms. Pierson had misappropriated investor funds, including their own, “to fund her lavish lifestyle,” the lawsuit said, including to pay for a $60,000-a-month apartment in New York City.

After The Cut published its article the next month, the investors sent Ms. Gomez, Ms. Teefey and Ms. Pierson a notice of rescission and demanded a return of their investment funds. Ms. Teefey “never substantively responded to the notice,” the lawsuit claims.

The lawsuit says that Ms. Teefey contacted Andrew Resnick, one of the investors, and suggested that he and the other plaintiffs should hold off on any lawsuit because Wondermind was setting up an escrow account to facilitate the return of their investment.

Ms. Teefey then “disappeared,” according to the lawsuit. The “bizarre interaction reinforces the lengths to which the defendants have gone — and will continue to go — to conceal their fraud, lull the plaintiffs, and evade accountability,” it said.

In April, Ms. Teefey told the investors in an email that she “thought we had returned your investment,” according to the lawsuit, when Wondermind “had returned nothing.”

The plaintiffs are seeking a full jury trial.

item.title: Senate Hopeful in Alaska Says ‘No Thanks’ to Kamala Harris’s Support
item.description:
For former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, to win the Senate race in Alaska this year, she would have to drastically outperform former Vice President Kamala Harris’s showing in the state in the 2024 presidential election.

So after Ms. Harris, who lost Alaska by 14 percentage points, signed a recent fund-raising email from her PAC supporting Ms. Peltola, Republicans saw an opening for an attack — and pounced. Ms. Peltola’s campaign, in turn, quickly said it had not approved the appeal and did not seek the former vice president’s endorsement.

In the fund-raising appeal, sent Wednesday, Ms. Harris urged supporters to “stand behind Mary,” describing the battle in Alaska as a “must-win race” for Democrats in their quest to reclaim the Senate. The well-funded Ms. Peltola is running as an independent-minded centrist against Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska. Limited polling suggests the race is competitive.

The email from Ms. Harris’s political action committee links to a donation page for a Democratic PAC and urges supporters to split their donations between Ms. Peltola’s campaign and Ms. Harris’s committee. It says: “If there’s anyone who can flip Alaska and secure the Senate majority for Democrats — it’s Mary.”

A day after the email went out, the campaign arm of Senate Republicans, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, moved to tie Ms. Peltola to Ms. Harris. A spokesman for the group, Nick Puglia, declared in a statement that Ms. Peltola had worked “hand in hand with Kamala Harris to put Alaska last, so it’s no surprise that Harris is backing Peltola.” (Ms. Peltola’s brief tenure in Congress, a little more than two years, overlapped with the Biden administration.)

A spokesman for Mr. Sullivan’s campaign, Nate Adams, piled on, saying in a statement, “No matter how hard Mary Peltola tries to hide from the endorsement, Alaskans can see exactly whose team she and Kamala Harris are on.”

Ms. Peltola’s campaign pushed back.

“Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 — her focus is and always will be Alaska,” the campaign said in a statement that cited the support Ms. Peltola has captured from several Alaska labor groups.

The Peltola campaign said that it did not approve the email from Ms. Harris’s organization, and that it had no knowledge about it before it was sent out.

A representative for Ms. Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It was not the first fund-raising appeal Ms. Harris’s political action committee, the Fight for the People PAC, had sent trying to use Ms. Peltola’s candidacy to raise funds for its own coffers.

On Jan. 12, the day Ms. Peltola announced her run, the PAC sent a similar message to supporters. “This is the race that may determine control of the Senate,” the January email began. But the timing of the latest solicitation stood out with the state’s Aug. 18 nonpartisan primary just days away.

Ms. Peltola is widely expected to advance Tuesday to the November general election. Under Alaska’s election system, the top four candidates in the primary move on. But Primary Day will offer the candidates a spotlight to deliver their messages and set the stage for the general-election race, along with an audience that is likely to be paying closer attention.

Defending Republican attacks linking Ms. Peltola with Ms. Harris is probably not the message the candidate had in mind for this important moment.

The appeal by Ms. Harris’s group also arrived as she considers running for president again. In the spring, she told the Rev. Al Sharpton that she “might” run, and she has spent recent months making public appearances across the country.

Ms. Peltola did not endorse Ms. Harris in 2024. The former congresswoman’s campaign slogan this year is “fish, family and freedom.”

State Representative Rebecca Himschoot of Alaska, an independent, said the email from Ms. Harris’s group could be somewhat unhelpful for Ms. Peltola, but that it was just a small part of a deluge of messaging from outside Alaska flooding the Senate race.

“I pity the voters in Alaska this cycle: it’s tremendously manipulative, all the stuff we’re getting,” Ms. Himschoot said, even as she described the outreach by Ms. Harris’s organization as “really dumb.”

“She’s riding Mary Peltola’s coattails,” Ms. Himschoot added. “And she’s not even running for anything that anyone knows of yet, and didn’t do well here to begin with.”

Alaska has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly two decades, though the state has an independent streak and has showed signs of shifting toward Democrats in some recent election cycles.

Most Alaska voters are politically unaffiliated. Senator Lisa Murkowski, a centrist Republican, won re-election in the state in 2022 by beating a Trump-backed rival.

Republicans also worry that the arrival in the race of another Dan Sullivan, a former elementary-school teacher with no political experience, will confuse supporters of the senator with the same name, potentially siphoning away some of his votes and lifting Ms. Peltola to victory.

Republicans have claimed that Ms. Peltola’s campaign planted the second Mr. Sullivan in the race to trick voters, but the Peltola campaign has denied coordinating with him. That Mr. Sullivan waged to a successful court battle to remain on the ballot after elections officials tried to remove him.

item.title: Stock Trading by Lawmakers Becomes a Campaign Attack Line
item.description:
Since the day she began her campaign for Congress, Paige Cognetti, the Democratic mayor of Scranton, has centered her pitch to voters on the prodigious stock trading of the House Republican she is seeking to unseat, Representative Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania.

“This year he’s already made 600 trades,” Ms. Cognetti said in the announcement video for her campaign in September. “Sold Chinese stocks the week of a tariff. Buys missile stocks before a war. Buys jet stocks before a big contract. Oversees crypto? Buys crypto stocks before a vote.”

It may be the district where the issue rings the loudest. Democrats are running ads highlighting how Mr. Bresnahan profited from a data center development by trading stocks related to the industry, and recent polls show Ms. Cognetti with a narrow lead. But she is not alone in zeroing in on stock trading by members of Congress as a potent line of attack in this year’s midterm elections.

Like many members of Congress who trade substantial amounts of stock, Mr. Bresnahan, the wealthy former chief executive of an electrical contracting company, has said he relies on a financial adviser to make his trades and never knows about the transactions before they happen or when they occur.

Mr. Bresnahan’s campaign said that Ms. Cognetti’s descriptions of his trades were “lies” and that he has “taken legitimate steps to ban congressional stock trading.”

Still, at a time when many voters are experiencing economic hardship and have grown increasingly suspicious that the political system is rigged, the mere possibility that a member of Congress could be profiting from the job has become politically toxic.

Roughly a quarter of legislators on Capitol Hill have traded individual stocks this term, with some buying and selling millions of dollars in shares. Since the start of this term in January 2025, members and their families have collectively traded $160 million to $664 million in individual stocks, according to a New York Times analysis of data collected from members’ required financial filings by 2iQ Research, an analytics firm.

An overwhelming majority of voters in both parties view stock trading by lawmakers with great suspicion and say they support barring them from doing so. The public backlash has fueled efforts by members of both parties, so far unsuccessful, to enact new legislation banning the practice.

In the meantime, both sides are leveraging the issue in the fight for control of Congress.

Democrats and Republicans alike are seeking to weaponize incumbents’ trades, particularly those where they can show the appearance of a conflict of interest, and putting them at the forefront of ads and campaign attacks in the country’s most competitive districts. It is a way to portray their opponents as corrupt and out of touch with the financial realities of working-class Americans.

In Northern New Jersey’s competitive Seventh Congressional District, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has been targeting Representative Thomas H. Kean Jr. for continuing to trade stocks while missing more than 100 votes during an extended absence for what he later said was treatment for depression. Mr. Kean’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

In Virginia, Democrats are attacking Representative Rob Wittman for trading more than $2.5 million in stocks between 2015 and 2023 while serving in Congress — including buying defense stocks like Lockheed Martin and Honeywell while serving on the Armed Services Committee.

“There’s a vicious cycle in Washington: Politicians trade stocks in the industries they’re supposed to regulate, then protect those industries instead of you,” said the caption with a campaign video that his opponent, Shannon Taylor, a prosecutor, posted online. “Let’s ban congressional stock trading — for good.”

(An outside group supporting Mr. Wittman apparently views this line of attack as effective: This week, it began running an ad highlighting his vote for a watered-down stock trading bill that passed the House passed in July, noting that he voted to put an end to the “greed and corruption” of “fat cat lawmakers.”) Mr. Wittman’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Republicans have also identified the issue as resonant with their voters.

In New York’s competitive Third Congressional District on Long Island, Michael J. LiPetri Jr., a Republican former state assemblyman, routinely attacks the Democrat he is running to unseat, Representative Tom Suozzi, for “the millions he’s pocketed from stock trading in Congress.”

Mr. Suozzi made nearly 600 stock trades involving 161 companies totaling as much as $24 million when he served in Congress between 2017 and 2023, according to public filings. In 2021, he faced an ethics investigation for failing to report about 300 stock trades in the required 45-day window. The House Ethics Committee later cleared him after concluding that it was not a willful violation, but a mistake.

A spokeswoman for Mr. Suozzi said all of his purchases were made at the discretion of his broker, without his direct input. She added that he has stopped purchasing stock altogether since returning to Congress in 2024, although he has sold some.

And in Nevada, Marty O’Donnell, a Trump-endorsed Republican running against Representative Susie Lee, a Democrat, often highlights Ms. Lee’s stock trades, claiming that she “has used her office to enrich herself with information the rest of us don’t have.” He has pledged that “unlike Susie, I will not trade stocks while representing Nevada in Congress.”

Ms. Lee, who was married to the chief executive of Full House Resorts, which operates casino facilities, has traded up to $2.8 million worth of stock since her divorce in 2024.

A spokeswoman for Ms. Lee said that all trades done before her divorce were executed by a money manager or her ex-husband. Since the divorce, Ms. Lee “received stocks as part of her divorce settlement and committed to divesting from them, which involves the selling of individual stocks in order to invest in other allowable instruments, like E.T.F.s and mutual funds,” the spokeswoman said, referring to exchange-traded funds.

In one instance where a former lawmaker is running for her old seat, an incumbent is trying to use the attack that is typically employed by a challenger.

Representative Jen Kiggans, Republican of Virginia, frequently accuses her opponent, former Representative Elaine Luria, of “insider stock trading” during her four years in Congress. Ms. Kiggans’s campaign did not point to any instances of insider trading, which is illegal, when asked about the allegations.

Instead, the campaign highlighted Ms. Luria’s previous opposition to a congressional stock trading ban (she now supports one). And it noted that Ms. Luria owns between $5 million and $25 million in NVIDIA stock, which she held when she voted for a $280 billion industrial policy bill enacted in 2022 that provided tens of billions of dollars for semiconductor manufacturing and research.

A spokesman for Ms. Luria dismissed Ms. Kiggans’s attacks as “lies,” and said that the bill in question did not increase her stock value. “Elaine supports banning congressional stock trading and preventing politicians from using their public offices for private gain,” he said.

The campaign trail focus comes as House Republicans have recently pushed through a bill that would impose some restrictions on lawmakers who trade stock, but stops short of a more stringent ban backed by a bipartisan coalition.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, has promised to bring the bipartisan alternative to the floor if Democrats win control of the House next year.

Donald K. Sherman, the chief executive of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a Democratic-aligned watchdog group, said it was not surprising to see the attacks on the practice coming from both political parties, because the issue is more salient than some others in government.

“You don’t need to be an ethics expert to understand it,” Mr. Sherman said. “An individual member of Congress can have an impact on a stock price, whether it’s tough questions at a hearing or an oversight hearing or confirmation of a particular cabinet secretary.”

Former Representative Tom Malinowski, Democrat of New Jersey, whose political career ended in part because he did not properly disclose dozens of stock trades, said a stock trading ban would do little to address far more serious issues that have eroded the public’s trust in political leaders.

“Stock trading by members of Congress should be banned, but it’s still a very poor substitute for attacking the real sources of corruption in Washington: unlimited dark money and Trump’s blatant selling of the presidency,” Mr. Malinowski said in an interview. “Those are significantly bigger problems. But candidates have seized on it as an all-purpose explanation for corruption.”

Olivia Diaz and Andrea Fuller contributed reporting.

item.title: Here Are the Biggest Stock Traders in Congress
item.description:
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are facing increasing voter pressure to ban congressional stock trading, a practice that has long given members an ability to profit from their access to market-moving information in closed-door meetings.

Roughly a quarter of legislators on Capitol Hill have traded individual stocks this term, with some buying and selling millions of dollars in shares. Since the start of this term in January 2025, members and their families have collectively traded $160 million to $664 million in individual stocks, according to a New York Times analysis of data collected from members’ required financial filings by 2iQ Research, an analytics firm.

Members are required to disclose their trades. But instead of declaring precise values, they report their trades in broad ranges, making it difficult to determine with precision how much stock they bought and sold.

A law passed in 2012, the STOCK Act, emphasizes that insider trading is illegal among lawmakers, as it is for the general public, and requires them to periodically disclose trades of shares held by them and members of their families. Existing laws do not prohibit lawmakers from trading individual stocks and do little in terms of enforcement. Critics of the system say that creates potential conflicts of interest and leaves open the possibility of members profiting from knowledge about legislation and nonpublic committee briefings.

Over the years, members of both parties have introduced bills cracking down on congressional stock trading, with some proposals more stringent than others. Last month, the House passed legislation limiting the ability of members, their spouses and their dependents to trade individual stocks, though it would allow lawmakers to keep the shares they already own and carve out exemptions for trusts and some other assets.

Nearly all Democrats opposed the bill after Republicans added an unrelated measure requiring voters to present photo identification in federal elections. Its prospects in the Senate are uncertain.

Here are the five lawmakers who have disclosed the largest individual stock trades made by them and their families, according to the Times analysis, based on the maximum dollar amount of their transactions reported since the start of this term on Jan. 3, 2025, through early August.

Mr. Khanna’s family traded shares valued at about $24 million to $147 million, according to the Times analysis.

The representative, first elected in 2016, disclosed that his family has traded about 7,200 times this term, the data reported as of Aug. 12 shows.

Mr. Khanna has said that he supported one version of a congressional ban, and that neither he nor his family directly make trades. His office declined to comment for this article but pointed to previous instances in which he has explained that his family’s finances are handled by outside advisers.

“My household’s only investments are held in a diversified trust my in-laws set up before marriage for my wife and children, managed independently by a third-party trustee,” he wrote in a May newsletter.

Under some proposals for stricter trading limits, members and their families would have to divest their blind trusts. The House bill that passed in July, which Mr. Khanna voted against, carved out an exemption for them. Most proposals have some exemptions for family trusts.

The former speaker has reported trades of shares valued at nearly $18 million to about $84 million across 17 transactions since the beginning of this congressional session. Paul Pelosi, Ms. Pelosi’s husband and a venture capitalist, owns each of the stocks traded. Two 2025 sales in particular were valued at a combined $10 million to $50 million in Apple stock.

A spokesman for Ms. Pelosi said in a statement that she “does not own any stocks and has no knowledge or subsequent involvement in any transactions.”

The “Pelosi Tracker” app has for years logged Mr. Pelosi’s investments and allowed its users to mimic his trades. Republicans in Congress have long singled out Ms. Pelosi for criticism for her family’s investments.

After initial hesitation, Ms. Pelosi said in recent years that she would support a congressional ban on stock trading. In July, she voted against the partisan House bill.

Mr. McCaul’s family bought and sold between $28 million and $75 million in individual stocks since January 2025, over the course of more than 1,100 transactions. All individual stock trades disclosed by Mr. McCaul came from his spouse, Linda Mays McCaul, according to the data. Mr. McCaul’s lawyer, Elliot Berke, said in a statement that a third-party manager makes the purchases without Ms. Mays McCaul’s direction.

One of Ms. Mays McCaul’s largest trades occurred last June when she sold between $500,000 and $1 million worth of shares in Nvidia, the California-based chip-making giant.

In July, Mr. McCaul voted in support of the House bill prohibiting the purchase of new individual stocks. Mr. McCaul, elected to the House in 2004, is retiring at the end of his term and is not up for re-election to his Austin-area district.

Mr. Shreve, a freshman member, traded between $16 million and nearly $42 million worth of shares through about 550 trades in 2025. The office of Mr. Shreve, who had run a company that built storage facilities across the Midwest, said last year that he would stop trading individual stocks. The data shows that neither he nor his family has traded individual stocks since then.

The shift came after a report by the publication NOTUS revealed that Mr. Shreve had made over 100 stock trades worth millions in the days after President Trump imposed sweeping tariffs on imports from many U.S. trading partners. Mr. Shreve’s chief of staff, Jeff Bishop, said on Thursday that trading activity occurred within a trust managed by a third party, which the representative set up to make charitable donations.

Mr. Shreve voted in support of the House’s Republican-led bill banning stock trading.

Mr. Armstrong traded about $8 million to $41 million worth of shares across nearly 700 individual trades.

He was appointed to the Senate in March after Markwayne Mullin resigned to become the new homeland security secretary. A former energy executive, Mr. Armstrong made the bulk of his trades during the week he was sworn in, the data shows.

At the time of his appointment, Mr. Armstrong led the board of directors at Williams Companies, a giant natural gas pipeline operator based in Tulsa, Okla. In June, Mr. Armstrong and his spouse sold between $5 million and $25 million in Williams stock, according to a financial filing.

The senator’s office said in a statement on Friday that the trades stemmed from a fund that Mr. Armstrong had no direction over. His spokeswoman noted that Mr. Armstrong had an annual salary of $750,000 before becoming a senator, and is now making a fraction of that.

“The focus should be on the folks that have built wealth while making a salary of $174,000 per year,” his spokeswoman wrote, referring to the allotted compensation for most members of Congress.

Mr. Armstrong will leave the Senate at the end of his term in January.

Andrea Fuller contributed reporting.

item.title: John Carro, Jurist Who Had Early Brush With Lee Harvey Oswald, Dies at 98
item.description:
John Carro, a prominent New York jurist who as a young probation officer in the Bronx tried to help a 13-year-old chronic truant named Lee Harvey Oswald a decade before Mr. Oswald was accused of assassinating President John F. Kennedy, died on July 26 at his home in Suffern, N.Y. He was 98.

His son John S. Carro confirmed the death.

Justice Carro spent 25 years on the bench in New York, after working as a police officer, social worker and mayoral aide. Most notably, he was the first Puerto Rican named to the First Department of the State Supreme Court’s Appellate Division, which hears appeals from state trial courts in Manhattan and the Bronx.

Rolando T. Acosta, a Dominican immigrant who was the presiding judge of the Appellate Division’s First Department from 2017 to 2023, said he was inspired to become a lawyer after hearing Mr. Carro speak at his high school in the Bronx in 1975.

“I had just emigrated in 1969, and here was this very eloquent Puerto Rican guy with an accent like mine,” he said in an interview. “I was in awe of him, speaking about the impact of the legal profession. I found myself in him.”

Before Justice Carro became a lawyer, he was a probation officer in children’s court in the Bronx. In 1953, he met Mr. Oswald, who had missed more than 40 days of school and had been sent for a psychological assessment.

During Mr. Carro’s testimony to the Warren Commission in 1964 — which concluded that Mr. Oswald was the lone gunman who killed Mr. Kennedy in Dallas on Nov. 22, 1963 — he recalled how he learned that Mr. Oswald had been charged as the assassin.

“A friend of mine called me up, a social worker, to tell me, ‘Carro, you know who that case is?’” he told the commission. “‘And he said, ‘That was the case you handled. Don’t you remember?’”

As they talked, Mr. Carro recalled feeling numb.

At the time of his testimony, he was an assistant to Mayor Robert F. Wagner, and he offered a largely empathetic portrait of Mr. Oswald, describing him as a desperately lonely boy from Texas living with an ineffectual mother, Marguerite, in a small Bronx apartment. Classmates taunted him for the way he spoke and dressed. Without friends, he watched television and read magazines all day.

“He felt he wasn’t learning anything in school and that he had other, more important things to learn and do,” Mr. Carro testified.

When asked by Wesley Liebeler, an assistant counsel to the commission, if he could have predicted that Mr. Oswald, at 13, would have been capable of committing a violent act like the assassination, he would not speculate.

“It is hard to say what motivated him,” he told the commission. “I don’t really know. I had no inkling of that at that stage.”

Mrs. Oswald, who refused to cooperate with efforts to find help for her son, took him to New Orleans in 1954 before Mr. Carro was able to find an institution where he could get psychiatric care.

Not long after, Mr. Carro left the job for a brief stint with the New York City Police Department.

“They kept wanting me to do undercover and narcotics work in Puerto Rican neighborhoods,” he told The Daily News in 1977, “and all I wanted to do was work with the juvenile division. So I quit after a month and got a job with the Youth Board.”

Juan Francisco Carro was born on Aug. 21, 1927, in Orocovis, Puerto Rico, to Juan and Josefina (Torres) Carro. Following his parents’ divorce, he moved to the United States with his mother, a seamstress, and they settled in the Bronx. He adopted the name John soon after arriving.

After high school, he enlisted in the Navy in 1945, serving as a pharmacist’s mate for two years. He received a bachelor’s degree from Fordham University in 1949.

In 1956, after three years of night classes, he earned a law degree from Brooklyn Law School and went to work for the social services agency Mobilization for Youth.

Starting in 1961, as an assistant to Mayor Wagner, he ran the city’s mobile information center and worked on minority programs. In 1964, he lost his bid for a Congressional seat in the Bronx in the Democratic primary.

His judicial career began in 1969 when Mayor John V. Lindsay named him to the criminal court in the Bronx. There, he angered the Bronx district attorney, Mario Merola, by dismissing a case in 1975 against two robbery suspects because police officers had violated their constitutional rights.

Victims have rights, Mr. Merola told The New York Times, “and these rights cannot be taken away by any possible legality by the police.”

His decision also angered the police union, and Justice Carro subsequently met with hundreds of its members to discuss the rights of defendants.

He was appointed to the Appellate Division in 1979 and served until 1994. Senator Daniel P. Moynihan of New York nominated him for a seat on the federal bench in 1988, but Justice Carro angrily withdrew his name after three years of inaction by the administrations of President Ronald Reagan and President George H.W. Bush.

In a meeting with Edwin Meese III, the U.S. attorney general, he was told, “You’re really not our kind of guy,” his son John said in an interview.

After losing the chance to be a U.S. District Court judge, Justice Carro urged Senator Moynihan, a Democrat, to name another Puerto Rican to the position. Mr. Moynihan did — and it turned out to be Sonia Sotomayor, whom the Senate unanimously confirmed in 1992. She was confirmed as the first Hispanic Supreme Court justice in 2009.

In 1993, Justice Carro was a leading candidate for a seat on the state Court of Appeals. But he withdrew after Gov. Mario M. Cuomo’s nominating panel learned that he had omitted from his application a son he had fathered during a relationship between his divorce and remarriage to the same woman. Newsday reported at the time that the son, whom it did not name, was in his 20s.

Justice Carro told The Associated Press that he had included information about the son on previous judicial applications but had inadvertently left it off the application for the Court of Appeals job. His son John said that the other son was listed on tax returns and that child support had been paid.

A year later, Justice Carro retired and started a law firm with John.

In addition to his son John, Justice Carro’s survivors include his wife, Terry (Parco) Carro, whom he first married in 1947; two other sons, Robert and Gregory, who are also lawyers; four daughters, Sherry Herlihy, Christine Riendeau, Lorna Sackler and Monique Carro, a lawyer; eight grandchildren; and five great-grandchildren.

His son Gregory, a State Supreme Court justice, is presiding over the murder trial of Luigi Mangione, who is accused of fatally shooting Brian Thompson, the chief executive of United Healthcare.

In 1998, after Gregory Carro’s swearing in as a criminal court judge, Justice Carro reflected on his own career as a liberal jurist and a leader in the Latino legal community.

“I was never afraid to speak out, and correct injustices, and do what I thought was right,” he told The Times. “Greg is more Americanized — the kids never had that whole involvement in the Latino community. I have so much respect for him. But it’s a whole different world.”
