item.title: Trump Dismisses Reports About Dire Conditions Aboard U.S. Aircraft Carrier
item.description:
President Trump on Friday dismissed concerns about dire conditions reported aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, an aircraft carrier that has been deployed for more than eight and a half months, much of it in support of the war against Iran.

Mr. Trump’s comments came in response to a reporter who asked about the reported conditions stemming from the extended deployment, which have included shortages of basic supplies, safety and hygiene issues and deteriorating mental health. When the reporter said that the crew members’ families were concerned, Mr. Trump said, “No, they’re not.”

The president, who was about to depart the Washington area for an event in New York, was asked whether he was concerned about the crew’s mental health and whether he thought the deployment had gone on too long.

“No. No. No,” he said. “Not nearly long enough.”

He acknowledged, however, that the Navy would soon replace the vessel “with another very similar ship.”

The Navy is sending the aircraft carrier George Washington to relieve the Lincoln, according to a U.S. official who spoke on the condition of anonymity for lack of authorization to speak publicly about ship schedules.

Mr. Trump’s remarks were the latest to downplay the consequences of his decision to attack Iran, causing a conflict that has lasted far longer than he initially promised and whose objectives and end have grown more and more elusive.

Mr. Trump has cast the war as a showing of American might. In his multiple declarations of victory, he has detailed successful missions that he claims wiped out Iran’s military capabilities.

He has consistently minimized the costs of the war, including the 18 U.S. servicemembers killed and hundreds of others wounded. He has compared the toll to previous, far longer and more deadly wars, like Vietnam, to argue that the Iran conflict has been relatively bloodless on the U.S. side.

The Defense Department even sought to remove four U.S. casualties from its death count just days after their deaths, a decision an official told The New York Times was in part to disassociate their deaths from the war in Iran because Mr. Trump had declared a cease-fire before they died, in April (though hostilities continued in the weeks after). The Pentagon has also at points withheld the full number of troops injured in the war.

Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, early this week also dismissed reports about the grim conditions aboard the U.S.S. Lincoln, saying the situation had been “misrepresented.”

In a letter on Thursday to Mr. Hegseth and Hung Cao, the Navy’s acting secretary, Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut, outlined issues reported on the ship.

“There have been widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns and disruptions in the mail system, which have caused many care packages in route to the ship to be lost in transit for months,” he wrote about the problems, many of which were reported earlier by Navy Times and Stars and Stripes.

Later on Friday, while speaking at an event in Garden City, N.Y., Mr. Trump continued to defend the war and boast about its progress.

“Pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” he told the crowd, referring to a critical maritime route for global oil supplies that Iran effectively blocked over the course of the war. The struggle over control of the strait has rattled global markets, impacted the energy supply and disrupted Mr. Trump’s efforts to end the conflict.

Mr. Trump also asserted, as he has in the past, that his goal — to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon — was worth the burdens placed on American, whose wallets have been hit by the rise in the price of gas and other increasing costs rippling out from the war.

“So remember that — when you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK,” he said. “I’ll never apologize. I did the right thing.”

John Ismay, Maggie Haberman and Karoun Demirjian contributed reporting.

item.title: Can an 80-Year-Old Senator Outrun the Age Issue?
item.description:
The sun was hot. The crowd had thinned. The ceremonial shovels, their duty done, rested in ceremonial dirt.

And Senator Ed Markey, 80, needed a quick favor from two other Massachusetts Democrats as they celebrated the opening of an industrial campus in Worcester: Would they join him for a selfie video?

“We’re at the groundbreaking! For GreenTech Park! Here in Worcester!” Markey said into the phone, treading lightly on the R in “park” and practically levitating off the pockmarked road as Representative Jim McGovern and Mayor Joseph Petty of Worcester, both 66, squeezed into the frame. “It’s the dawn of a new era!”

That was yesterday. By this morning, that selfie video had been packaged into a Instagram reel that also showed Markey bounding through an awards ceremony and into the local minor league baseball stadium that night — a daily display of vim from an octogenarian who insists he has the vigor for another six-year term.

Markey’s challenge: Across the country, Democratic voters are eagerly swapping aging lawmakers for younger challengers. After Representative John Larson, 78, of Connecticut, lost his race for a 15th term to former Mayor Luke Bronin, 47, of Hartford this week, I drove up to Worcester to see how Markey, the oldest Senate Democrat running for re-election, is trying to defy that trend.

His approach: Markey is facing a challenge from Representative Seth Moulton, a 47-year-old moderate. Markey has seized on the ideological dimensions of the race, running on his progressive bona fides with a similar playbook to the one that helped him beat former Representative Joe Kennedy III in 2020. He might also be betting that a willingness to be seen pounding the pavement — and his support from young voters — will help him seem more Bernie than Biden.

“I always think of myself as the youngest guy in the room,” he told me yesterday, “when it comes to ideas.”

At Polar Park, the AAA baseball stadium for the Red Sox feeder team that Massachusetts wrested from Rhode Island in the late 2010s, he greeted local dignitaries (the 31-year-old mayor of Gardner, Mass.! The owner of Sullivan Tire!) like celebrities.

Then he and McGovern slipped into the broadcasting booth, where Markey spouted off trivia about the most promising players on the team.

“Honestly,” he said as a player named Franklin Arias stepped to the plate, “we’re seeing the growth of the new Mookie Betts.”

As he walked through the stadium, he paused to take in a display of team programs going all the way back to 1973 — the year that Markey first took office in the Massachusetts State House. (He was elected to Congress three years later, and served there until he was elected to the Senate in a special election in 2013.)

Moulton, a six-term congressman from Massachusetts’ North Shore, has made Markey’s status as a long-term fixture of Washington the central point of his campaign.

“People ought to ask, ‘What are you going to accomplish in the next six years that you haven’t been able to accomplish in the last 50?’” Moulton said at a debate in July.

Polling on the race is fairly scant. A University of New Hampshire poll from June showed Markey leading Moulton by six percentage points; worryingly for Markey, though, Moulton had increased his support by 12 points since February, while nearly a quarter of respondents remained undecided.

Markey has portrayed Moulton as being too moderate for Massachusetts, criticizing him for not supporting “Medicare for all” and for picking a fight with his party about transgender rights after the 2024 election. Markey’s betting that the age argument doesn’t work if a younger candidate isn’t seen as sufficiently liberal.

“Whether it’s Minnesota with Peggy Flanagan, or Michigan with Abdul El-Sayed, or here in Massachusetts, it’s progressives versus moderates, and the progressives are winning,” Markey said.

The argument has worked once before. It carried Markey to victory over Kennedy — particularly after the senator drew hordes of young volunteers, a group that called themselves the Markeyverse, to his campaign. Some of those volunteers are on his staff today, cutting his videos and increasing his TikTok following.

“You have to move to where the next generation is. You have to go to them,” Markey said at the baseball park, as the sun set and the sound of a hit crackled in the air.

He has promised to make way for the next generation if he wins in November; he said after the July debate that he would step down after one more term, when he will be 86.

item.title: Navy Carrier’s Problems Are Tied to Attacks on U.S. Base Early in War
item.description:
The aircraft carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln’s supply problems began soon after the first day of the war, as Iranian missiles and attack drones fell on a Navy base in Bahrain.

The Iranian attack, retaliation for the U.S.-Israeli assault on Tehran, destroyed much of the base. And as it went up in smoke, so did a major logistics hub that the Navy has relied on for decades.

The Navy needed a Plan B to continue feeding the sailors working around the clock to keep warplanes flying strike missions, and later to maintain a blockade of Iran’s ports.

With the threat of Iranian attacks at other ports in the region, the Pentagon looked to a base under British command on the island of Diego Garcia as its supply hub, which is south of the Maldives and roughly 2,200 miles from where two aircraft carrier strike groups have been operating in the Gulf of Oman.

The loss of the hub in Bahrain has contributed to a host of reported problems on carriers supporting operations against Iran, as Democratic senators raise concerns about the Lincoln’s 5,000 sailors and their nearly nine-month deployment.

Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut, said in a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that the reported problems included shortages of basic supplies and the deteriorating mental health of its crew members.

On Friday at a military air base in Maryland, Mr. Trump dismissed those concerns. “That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another, very similar, ship,” he said.

The Lincoln’s replacement is the Japan-based carrier U.S.S. George Washington, which earlier this week was heading west through the Strait of Malacca in Indonesian waters en route to the Middle East.

Another carrier, the U.S.S. George H.W. Bush, has been operating in the Middle East for months since deploying from Norfolk on March 31.

When asked if the carrier deployments were too long, the president said, “No, no, no, not nearly long enough.”

Mr. Hegseth had a similar response on Thursday when a reporter asked how long the United States could maintain its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

“We can hold it as long as we need to, indefinitely,” he replied.

At the war’s outset, Keir Starmer, then the British prime minister, denied the Pentagon access to Diego Garcia for use in the operation against Iran. That decision drew Mr. Trump’s ire, and Mr. Starmer ultimately relented on March 1, granting the U.S. military access to the island for what he described as a “specific and limited defensive purpose.”

A U.S. military official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive logistics, said the Navy began using Diego Garcia as the main shipment point shortly after the Navy’s base in Bahrain was heavily damaged.

The use of Diego Garcia as the Navy’s new logistics hub may explain why Iran fired two medium-range ballistic missiles at the island on March 20.

One of the missiles fell into the Indian Ocean short of its target. A Navy warship shot down the other.

The San Diego-based Lincoln has been at sea for nearly nine months without what the Navy calls a “liberty port” — where sailors can get off the ship for a few days.

Bahrain is one of the two ports where U.S. aircraft carriers in the region have typically moored so their crews can get some downtime. The other, the Emirati port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, is also well within the range of Iranian missiles.

The Trump administration relied on yet another carrier, the U.S.S. Gerald R. Ford, in the Caribbean for its pressure campaign against Venezuela and later extended its deployment to the Middle East to launch airstrikes against Iran. So far the war has seen the commitment of a significant portion of the Navy’s fleet of aircraft carriers, which will go down to 10 with the expected retirement of U.S.S. Nimitz next year.

While six months is the typical length of a Navy deployment at sea in peacetime, some carriers have done far longer stretches at following the Sept. 11 attacks. The Ford’s 326-day deployment, however, broke the record for the longest by a carrier since the Vietnam War.

But in that war, carriers assigned to Yankee Station, a section of the Pacific off the coast of Vietnam, would often head to the Navy base at Subic Bay, Philippines — a short two-day transit away — where sailors could take a break from running nonstop flight operations and the ship could load up on ordnance, food, fuel and other necessary supplies.

By tradition and Navy regulation, the commanding officer of a warship can request a “beer day” for their crews when they have been at sea for 45 straight days or longer. Given the Lincoln’s time at sea, the crew would have been eligible for five beer days already.

A spokesman for the U.S. Fifth Fleet, which covers naval operations in region and would authorize beer days, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday about whether any of the ships participating in the Iran war had requested them.

In an interview, Representative Mike Levin, Democrat of California, said that his constituents included sailors aboard the Lincoln, and that their family members had reached out to express their concerns about the deployment.

“It gets back to that big picture, which is: What is the mission here?” Mr. Levin said. “That’s what the families want to know.”

item.title: President Trump Takes Credit for Steep Crime Rate Declines
item.description:
President Trump took credit on Friday for what he said is the nation’s “best crime record in recorded history,” pointing to new crime data on 2025 released by the F.B.I. on Friday.

The president said that “every single number” in the report was the lowest in recorded history, which is not the case. While the president made sweeping, exaggerated claims, crime analysts agree that 2025 was a remarkable year, with record declines and historically low crime rates.

“The 2025 murder rate is tied with 1955 and 1956 for the lowest rate since F.B.I. estimations began in 1936,” the new F.B.I. report says. Independent analysts have gone further, questioning the accuracy of the 1950s estimates and saying that murder is most likely at the lowest rate ever recorded in crime and public health data.

Jeff Asher, an expert on crime statistics, wrote in a newsletter on Friday that the drops were not necessarily surprising, given the trends in recent years. “The bottom line is that the U.S. murder rate was lower last year than it has been in the lifetime of anyone born after Kennedy was elected president, and it’s plunging even lower in 2026,” he said.

Mr. Trump pointed to his administration’s efforts to limit immigration and increase deportations as one reason for the reductions. He also claimed that his personal support for law enforcement had helped bring about the change.

“Together we’re showing what is possible when you finally have a president in the White House who supports our police,” he said.

He said that federal intervention in Washington, Memphis and New Orleans had led to major crime declines in those places. “In Memphis, crime is down 71 percent. In New Orleans, crime is down 75 percent. And in D.C., crime is down 81 percent,” Mr. Trump said.

But drops of that scale are not reflected in the available data. In Washington, police department data shows that violent crime was down by 18 percent in 2025 compared wtih the year before. Crime this year in the capital is down 20 percent compared with the same period last year.

In New Orleans, murders declined by 3 percent, fatal shootings dropped 21 percent, armed robberies decreased 28 percent and carjackings dropped 35 percent from 2024 to 2025. So far this year, crime has ticked up 5 percent.

In Washington, the National Guard likely contributed to a decrease in property crimes, according to a June report from the Niskanen Center, a centrist think tank. But the same report said the Guard had barely any effect on violent crime. Robberies and homicides declined at roughly the same rates before and after the Guard arrived, the report found.

Memphis came closer to Mr. Trump’s numbers, reporting a decline of 27 percent in major crimes in 2025, and a further decline so far this year of 60 percent.

The decline in crime predates Mr. Trump’s current term in office. Crime spiked during the first years of the pandemic. There were also major street protests of police brutality and criticism of law enforcement.

But in 2022, during the Biden administration, violent crime began to subside. Carjackings and some types of property crime, like car theft, peaked a little later before beginning to decline.

Crime experts say that the picture has continued to improve in 2026, which is on track to reach new lows. But the causes, they cautioned, are unclear.

“That means lives saved, families spared trauma, and communities made safer — and it deserves to be celebrated,” said Adam Gelb, the president of the Council on Criminal Justice, a nonpartisan think tank. “But the reasons for the decline are much less clear than the decline itself.”
